newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Freight rates buoyant on Mideast oil sales to Asia.
newsitem.headline: Freight rates buoyant on Mideast oil sales to Asia.

text.p: Increasing crude oil sales by the Middle East to Asia and a rise in tanker demand are factors expected to keep tanker freight rates buoyant into the next century, industry experts said on Tuesday.
Tanker life expectancy was rising and the rate of scrapping was slowing down -- both likely to tighten the tanker market, the shipping experts said.

The Worldscale (WS) rate, an index used to assess freight costs, could rise to WS80 in 2000 for very large crude carriers (VLCC) from from WS50 in 1995, said John Russel, a consultant at London-based Petroleum Economics Ltd (PEL).
VLCC are tankers that carry at least 160,000 deadweight tons (dwt).
Russel said PEL forecast five-year time charter rates between 2000 and 2004 would rise to just more than WS90, from the current WS70.

Speaking at the World Tanker Outlook conference in Singapore, he said he expected surplus tanker volume in 2000 to drop to 28 million dwt from 44 million dwt in 1995 on increased demand for oil tankers. But while the surplus volume was expected to decline, the rate of ships being scrapped was also expected to fall, tightening the potential supply of freight.
The average lifespan of tankers is rising and now stands at 22 to 23 years, compared to a previous average of 19 years.
A projected increase in seaborne crude oil trade from the Middle East to the Asia-Pacific region starting from 1995 would also spur an increase in freight rates, Russel said.

Russel told the conference there had been an increase in the volume and direction of oil moving from the Mideast Gulf to Asia. He cited a 19 percent jump in volumes between 1993 and 1995 against a 15 percent cut in volumes from the Gulf to the West. By 2000, the volume would rise another 52 percent, Russel said.

"Because of the very strong growth in oil consumption in Asia-Pacific region and because the region itself has extremely limited availability ... we can anticipate a substantial increase in the amount of oil trading from the Arabian Gulf," he added.

Kamel Al Awadhi, a manager at Kuwait Oil Tanker S.A.K. planning and commercial affairs, said he was optimistic about the future. He told Reuters at the conference that the rise in oil demand from Asia would play into the hands of tanker owners and drive freight rates higher.

Russel also said some of the present Gulf oil supplies to the Atlantic seaboard were going to be diverted towards Asia, which would allow the Atlantic seaboard to absorb more of its own incremental oil output.
At the same time, there was also a very strong likelihood of continuing increases in the volume of West African crude being traded into Asia, he said.

He said the demand for 160 million dwt tankers would jump by 18.6 percent between 1995 and 2000, while demand for smaller size ships ranging between 10 million dwt and 45 million dwt would rise by 6.2 percent.
